traveler: Pantaleon of Nicomedia (Pantoleon; Saint Panteleimon, the All-Merciful; San Pantaleone)
title: The Physician Denounced by Physicians: Nicomedia, the Olive Tree, and the Scattering of the Blood
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Nicomedia, birth in the house of Eustorgius
stops.date_confidence: traditional. No document fixes the year; c. 275 is hagiographic tradition reported without a source by the Catholic Encyclopedia and by both the English and Spanish Wikipedia entries. Month and day are pin-forcing placeholders. The Nicomedia coordinate is inherited byte-identical from constantino_el_grande.journey.json and catorce_santos_ayudantes.journey.json.
stops.campa: In the eastern capital, in the house of Eustorgius, a rich pagan of Nicomedia, a son is born and named Pantoleon, in all things like a lion. His mother is Eubula, a Christian in a household that is not. The city he is born into is the seat of Diocletian's court, the address from which the empire is governed and from which the last persecution will shortly be ordered. No document records the year of the birth. The tradition gives it as about 275, and the tradition is all there is.
suggested_refs: The imperial capital quarter of Nicomedia, modern Izmit, seat of Diocletian's court

stops.name: Nicomedia, what Eubula does not finish
stops.date_confidence: traditional and undatable. The Catholic Encyclopedia says only that Eubula instructed him in early childhood and died young, giving no age for either of them. The year here is a placeholder inside that window.
stops.campa: Eubula teaches the boy the faith while she has him, in a house where the old gods are kept downstairs. Then she dies. The Catholic Encyclopedia records only that she instructed him in his childhood before her death, and gives no age for either of them. Eustorgius raises what is left of the household. The teaching goes cold within a few years, and the boy grows up in his father's religion, with his mother's half-lesson under it and nobody in the house to repeat it.
suggested_refs: The Christian minority households of Nicomedia before the persecution

stops.name: Nicomedia, the school of Euphrosinos
stops.date_confidence: traditional; the teacher's name is attested in the hagiographic tradition summarized by en.wikipedia and it.wikipedia, the year is a placeholder with no source behind it.
stops.campa: He is placed with Euphrosinos, a physician of standing in the imperial city, and learns the art of the body: the drugs, the compartmented box, the long-handled probe that painters will later put into his hand. He is good at it. Nothing in the training is Christian and nothing in it needs to be. Medicine at Nicomedia is a court profession, and a promising student of a court physician is on a track that ends inside the palace. He finishes the track.
suggested_refs: The medicine box and long-handled probe, his standing attributes in later iconography

stops.name: Nicomedia, physician to the emperor
stops.date_confidence: traditional. The appointment is in every version of the legend; the year is a placeholder. Which emperor is an open contradiction: the Catholic Encyclopedia and en.wikipedia name Maximian, it.wikipedia names Galerius, and neither acknowledges the other. Not resolved here.
stops.campa: He is taken into the imperial household as physician to the emperor. Which emperor is not settled. The Catholic Encyclopedia and the English tradition name Maximian, the Italian tradition names Galerius, and neither notices the other. The court he serves is a court already grinding toward the edict of 303, a physician who treats the men who will soon order the empire's Christians rounded up.
suggested_refs: The tetrarchic palace at Nicomedia, workplace of both the court physician and the young Constantine

stops.name: Nicomedia, Hermolaus asks what the learning is worth
stops.date_confidence: legend, undated. Hermolaus's rank is itself contested: the Catholic Encyclopedia and OrthodoxWiki call him a priest, en.wikipedia says he is characterized as a bishop of the church at Nicomedia in the later literature. The quotation reaches this file only through en.wikipedia's citation of Liguori; the Liguori original was not located.
stops.campa: Hermolaus, priest of the hidden church of Nicomedia and in the later literature a bishop, stops the young physician and asks what all his acquirements are worth if he does not know the science of salvation. Two other priests keep house with him, Hermippus and Hermocrates. Orthodox tradition will make all three of them survivors of a massacre of twenty thousand Christians in this city. The question is put to a man who can already cure most of what is brought to him, and it lands.
stops.quote: But, my friend, of what use are all thy acquirements in this art, since thou art ignorant of the science of salvation?
stops.quote_source: St. Alphonsus Liguori, Victories of the Martyrs, life of St. Pantaleon, quoted in the English Wikipedia article 'Saint Pantaleon'
suggested_refs: Liguori's Victories of the Martyrs, the secondary carrier of the Hermolaus rebuke

stops.name: Nicomedia, the child and the viper
stops.date_confidence: legend, undated. The episode comes from the Prologue and Menaion tradition as rendered by the Holy Trinity calendar; no source gives it a year and the pin date is a placeholder.
stops.campa: On a road in the city he finds a child dead of a snakebite, the viper still lying beside the body. He prays as Hermolaus has taught him to pray, in the name of Christ, and the account says the child gets up and the snake bursts apart. He has spent his life so far curing what can be cured, and the art he was trained in has no entry for this one. He goes back to the priest and is baptized, in Diocletian's own capital, a few years before the edict that will kill him.
stops.quote: The child revived, and the viper shattered into pieces before the eyes of Pantoleon.
stops.quote_source: Holy Trinity Russian Orthodox Church, Lives of the Saints, 27 July, Great Martyr and Healer Panteleimon
sources: Holy Trinity Russian Orthodox Church, Lives of the Saints, 27 July (holytrinityorthodox.com)
suggested_refs: The Prologue and Menaion account of the snakebitten child, the hinge of the conversion

stops.name: Nicomedia, the blind man and the father converted
stops.date_confidence: legend, undated. Correction carried: the research pool had this as a paralytic healed in a demonstration before the emperor. The checkable sources say a blind man, and say it converts his father. The paralytic version survives only in Bonaventure Hammer's 1908 devotional compilation and is not carried as event.
stops.campa: A blind man comes to him and he restores the sight, calling on the name of Christ over the eyes. Eustorgius is watching. The father who raised him in the old gods is converted by what he sees his son do, and dies not long after, leaving him the estate. The healing is often retold as a contest staged before the emperor over a paralytic on the ground. That version belongs to the devotional compilations. The sources that can be checked put a blind man in the room and a pagan father.
sources: Fr. Bonaventure Hammer, The Fourteen Holy Helpers (1908), Wikisource, for the rejected paralytic variant
suggested_refs: The two incompatible versions of the demonstrative healing, blind man and paralytic

stops.name: Nicomedia, the estate given away
stops.date_confidence: legend, undated. The inheritance, the freeing of the slaves and the free practice are all hagiographic tradition; the year is a placeholder set just before the persecution.
stops.campa: On his father's death he inherits the house, the land, and the slaves. He frees the slaves, sells what will sell, and hands the proceeds to the poor of Nicomedia. Then he goes on practising without a fee, treating whoever comes and visiting Christians already in the prisons. A court physician who charges nothing is a visible thing in a capital city. The colleagues he has left behind at the palace can see exactly how much of their trade is walking out the door.
stops.quote: devoted all his talent to serving the poor
suggested_refs: The free clinic of the converted court physician, and the prison visits

stops.name: Nicomedia, the church razed and the edict published
stops.date_confidence: attested. Lactantius dates the razing of the Nicomedia church to 23 February 303, the feast of the Terminalia, and the publication of the Edict against the Christians to the following day. Date and pin inherited byte-identical from saint_erasmus.journey.json, saint_acacius.journey.json and saint_blaise.journey.json. No source places Pantaleon at the posting; the link is thematic, not documentary.
stops.campa: On the feast of the Terminalia Diocletian has the new church at Nicomedia pulled down, and the Edict against the Christians is published the next morning: scripture burned, churches levelled, Christians in office stripped of rank. It goes out along every road the empire keeps. The same order carries off Blaise at Sebastea, Cyriacus on the Via Salaria, Acacius at Byzantium, and Erasmus in the east, four men who will stand beside Pantaleon in a German list eleven centuries later. He is in the city where it is posted.
suggested_refs: The imperial palace quarter at Nicomedia, where the edict of 303 was posted

stops.name: Nicomedia, the myriads of the eighteenth of March
stops.date_confidence: attested as a distinct calendar entry, Myriads of Holy Martyrs, by the sword, at Nicomedia, kept on 18 March. The year 303 is the persecution's year rather than the entry's. Its relation to the Pantaleon and Acacius dossiers is confusion in later calendars, not any documented link. Convention inherited from saint_acacius.journey.json.
stops.campa: A calendar entry keeps the Myriads of Holy Martyrs put to the sword at Nicomedia under the eighteenth of March. Orthodox tradition makes Hermolaus, Hermippus, and Hermocrates survivors of that killing, three priests left over from twenty thousand. The number is a calendar number, and the relation of this entry to the other Nicomedian dossiers is confusion in later books rather than any documented link. Pantaleon's teacher is walking the same streets on borrowed time.
sources: saint_acacius.journey.json, stop 'Nicomedia, the myriads of the eighteenth of March'
suggested_refs: The 18 March commemoration of the Myriads of Nicomedia, an unharmonized dossier

stops.name: Nicomedia, denounced by the physicians
stops.date_confidence: legend, undated. The Catholic Encyclopedia's martyr-legend summary gives envy of fellow court physicians as the mechanism; the year is a placeholder between the edict and the traditional date of death.
stops.campa: His former colleagues at the court go to the authorities and name him a Christian. The motive the sources give is envy, and the mechanism is the edict: a denunciation now has an office to go to and a penalty attached to it. He is arrested. The persecution has been running a year and its machinery no longer needs to look for anyone; it only needs to be told. A physician is turned in by physicians, and that is the one detail every version of the story keeps.
suggested_refs: The denunciation procedure created by the first edict of 303

stops.name: Nicomedia, brought before the emperor
stops.date_confidence: legend. The refusal to sacrifice is in every version; the speech is not Passio text but a 1908 devotional retelling by Bonaventure Hammer, and is quoted here as such. Which emperor sits in the chair is the same unresolved Maximian and Galerius contradiction as at the appointment.
stops.campa: He is brought in and told to sacrifice. The devotional retellings give him a speech in front of the throne: that the God he adores made heaven and earth and raised the dead, and that the emperor's idols are dead things which can do nothing. Those words come from a compilation of 1908, not from any Roman record. What the record keeps is the refusal and what follows it. The emperor who wants the sacrifice is the same one whose body his hands used to treat.
stops.quote: The God whom I adore is Jesus Christ. He created heaven and earth, He raised the dead to life, made the blind see and healed the sick, all through the power of His word. Your idols are dead, they can not do anything.
stops.quote_source: Fr. Bonaventure Hammer, The Fourteen Holy Helpers (1908), chapter on St. Pantaleon, Wikisource
sources: Fr. Bonaventure Hammer, The Fourteen Holy Helpers (1908), Wikisource
suggested_refs: Hammer's 1908 Fourteen Holy Helpers, the source of the throne speech

stops.name: Nicomedia, the torches and the lead
stops.date_confidence: legend, undated, and the order of the torments is not stable between sources. The Catholic Encyclopedia prints the catalogue and in the same entry calls the lives that carry it late in date and valueless. The month is a placeholder inside the traditional year of death.
stops.campa: The Passio begins its catalogue. They burn him with torches and the torches do not take. They heat a vessel of lead and lower him into it, and the legend says the lead cools around him. Each instrument is tried, each fails, and the text moves down its list to the next one. The Catholic Encyclopedia, printing the same catalogue, says of the lives that carry it that they are late in date and valueless, and then goes on defending the martyrdom itself.
stops.quote: the lives containing these legendary features are all late in date and valueless
suggested_refs: The Passio catalogue of failed torments, and the encyclopedia's judgment on it

stops.name: Nicomedia harbour, the stone that floats
stops.date_confidence: legend, undated. The coordinate approximates the ancient harbour shoreline of Nicomedia; no source fixes the point, and modern Izmit stands partly on filled ground where the Roman quays were.
stops.campa: They take him down to the water, tie a stone to him, and throw him off the harbour of Nicomedia into the gulf. The stone floats. He comes back to the shore, and they hand him on to the next method. The coordinate here approximates the ancient shoreline as closely as it can be placed; no source fixes the spot, and the modern city stands on filled ground where the Roman quays used to be. The sea is the third instrument tried on him and the third failure.
suggested_refs: The ancient harbour of Nicomedia on the gulf of Izmit

stops.name: Nicomedia, the beast pit
stops.date_confidence: legend, undated. Nothing in the surviving record confirms an arena, an animal, or a crowd at Nicomedia in this connection; the episode is Passio narrative only.
stops.campa: He is put into the arena with wild animals. The account says they will not touch him, that they lie down at his feet, and that the crowd on the benches starts shouting for his God instead of against it. The arena is the public instrument, the one built to be watched, and in the legend it is the one that converts the audience. Nothing in the surviving record confirms a crowd, an arena, or a single animal. The text needs a spectacle at this point, so it supplies one.
suggested_refs: The beast-pit episode, the converting spectacle of the Passio

stops.name: Nicomedia, the wheel
stops.date_confidence: legend, undated, and the position of the wheel in the sequence is contradictory. English Wikipedia's summary opens with a wheel set over fire and closes with the wheel again; the Catholic Encyclopedia orders the torments differently. Neither acknowledges the other.
stops.campa: They bind him to the wheel and turn it. The wheel breaks. In some tellings this is the first attempt, with the fire set beneath it; in others it is the last, after the sea and the beasts, and the sequence shifts from source to source without any of them noticing the shift. Six instruments have now been tried on one man. The executioners are left with the sword, which is the plainest tool they have and the only one of them the story will finally let work.
suggested_refs: The breaking wheel, his intermittent attribute in Western images

stops.name: Nicomedia, the olive tree
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The Catholic Encyclopedia dates the death about 305 and en.wikipedia gives c. 305; the specific calendar date 27 July 305 comes from it.wikipedia as tradition, not primary attestation. The 27 July feast is separately attested in both Western and Byzantine calendars.
stops.campa: They take him outside the city and bind him to an olive tree. The first stroke fails; the account says the sword melts like wax against him. He prays, a voice is heard, and he tells the executioners to finish it. Then he consents, and the head comes off. Tradition holds that milk ran from the body in place of blood, and that the olive, out of its season, came into fruit while he was still tied to it. The wood of that tree is afterward credited with healing power.
stops.quote_source: OrthodoxWiki, article 'Panteleimon', account of the failed beheading at the olive tree
suggested_refs: The olive tree of the execution, and the olive branch in his iconography

stops.name: Nicomedia, the name given at the block
stops.date_confidence: attested as tradition. The Catholic Encyclopedia, en.wikipedia and OrthodoxWiki all place the name Panteleimon at the death, awarded for the dying prayer of forgiveness. Correction carried: the research pool's geography lens placed it at baptism, contradicting its own cited sources and its own chronology lens.
stops.campa: He forgives the men who have spent the day trying to kill him, and the East gives him a second name for it. He was born Pantoleon, in all things like a lion. He dies Panteleimon, all-merciful. Some retellings move the name back to the baptism and make it the priest's gift, but the Catholic Encyclopedia and OrthodoxWiki both put it here, at the tree, awarded for the last thing he says. The lion's name is his father's choice, and it does not survive him.
stops.quote: When the saint was beheaded, the olive tree - to which the saint was tied, at the moment of his death was covered with fruit.
stops.quote_source: Holy Trinity Russian Orthodox Church, Lives of the Saints, 27 July, Great Martyr and Healer Panteleimon
sources: Holy Trinity Russian Orthodox Church, Lives of the Saints, 27 July
suggested_refs: The two names, Pantoleon at birth and Panteleimon at the block

stops.name: Nicomedia, Adamantius gathers the blood
stops.date_confidence: tradition, local to Ravello, and internally strained. it.wikipedia names Adamantius as a witness at the 305 execution, while the same Italian material elsewhere traces the Ravello custody chain to the twelfth century. The sources do not reconcile the eight-hundred-year gap and this file does not either.
stops.campa: Local tradition at Ravello names a witness at the execution, Adamantius, who gathers some of the blood up from the ground and keeps it. Everything the Amalfi coast will later venerate hangs on this man, and he appears in no source earlier than the Italian material that requires him to exist. The same tradition elsewhere puts his collecting in the twelfth century, eight hundred years after the killing, and does not notice that it has said both things at once.
suggested_refs: Adamantius, the named witness on whom the Ravello relic chain depends

stops.name: Nicomedia, the burial
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. Burial by fellow Christians is general hagiographic tradition in the English and Italian entries. The grave itself is not located by any source reached here, though Justinian's later rebuilding of a shrine on the site implies it was known in the sixth century.
stops.campa: Christians of the city take the body and bury it. From birth to grave he has not left Nicomedia; the whole recorded life fits inside one set of coordinates, and everything that happens to him after this happens to pieces of him, in other people's countries. The grave itself is not located by any source reached here, and none of them describes it. Two and a half centuries later an emperor will build over the site, which means that somebody still knew where it was.
suggested_refs: The unlocated grave of Pantaleon at Nicomedia

stops.name: Cyrrhus, Theodoret names him among the martyrs
stops.date_confidence: attested as the earliest literary testimony identified, cited by the Catholic Encyclopedia to Theodoret's eighth discourse on the martyrs; Theodoret dies about 457 and the year here is a placeholder inside his working life. The pin is the bishop's own see at Cyrrhus, explicitly not a Pantaleon site. Theodoret was not read directly.
stops.campa: Theodoret, bishop of Cyrrhus in Syria, names Pantaleon among the martyrs in the eighth of his discourses. It is the earliest literary testimony to the cult that this research could identify, roughly a century and a half after the death, and it says nothing about torches or lead or a floating stone. The pin is the bishop's own see, not a Pantaleon site. The Martyrologium Hieronymianum carries him too, compiled in the West at a place these sources do not fix.
sources: Catholic Encyclopedia (1913), 'St. Pantaleon', citing Theodoret and the Martyrologium Hieronymianum
suggested_refs: Theodoret's eighth discourse on the martyrs, and the Martyrologium Hieronymianum entry

stops.name: Nicomedia, Justinian rebuilds the shrine
stops.date_confidence: attested. Procopius records the rebuilding in De aedificiis, composed about 554 to 560; the year here is a placeholder inside Justinian's building programme. Correction carried: the research pool placed Procopius's testimony at Constantinople and counted it as a second, separate item. It is Nicomedia, and it is one testimony.
stops.campa: Procopius, writing the Buildings for Justinian, records that the emperor rebuilt the shrine of Pantaleon at Nicomedia. The Catholic Encyclopedia cites Procopius as an early witness to the cult without saying where the witness is pointing, and one lens of this research read the testimony as veneration at Constantinople. It is Nicomedia. The city that killed him is now spending imperial money on his roof, under a Christian emperor, two and a half centuries later.
suggested_refs: Procopius, De aedificiis, on Justinian's rebuilding of the Nicomedia shrine

stops.name: Constantinople, the phial that liquefies
stops.date_confidence: attested for the transfer and the phial by the Catholic Encyclopedia, but undated by it and by en.wikipedia; the year is an admitted placeholder. Correction carried: the research pool dated the transfer to the eighth century and added Carthage as a rival claimant, neither of which is in its cited source. Pin inherited byte-identical from constantino_el_grande.journey.json.
stops.campa: The relics are carried across the gulf to the capital at a date no source gives. In Constantinople a phial said to hold his blood is kept, and it is reported to liquefy on his feast day. This is the first appearance of the wet miracle that Ravello will later own outright, and the two claims never meet: the Catholic Encyclopedia puts the liquefaction here, the Italian sources put it on the Amalfi coast, and neither adjudicates. Constantine's city is now a relic warehouse.
suggested_refs: The Constantinopolitan phial of Pantaleon's blood, rival to the Ravello ampoule

stops.name: Tsri, the relics enter Caucasian Albania
stops.date_confidence: reported by a medieval chronicle, undated within it. Movses Kaghankatvatsi has Bishop Grigoris bring the relics to Tsri; Grigoris dies about 338 and the year here is a placeholder taken from that. The coordinates approximate a village near Barda, Azerbaijan; the exact site is not independently confirmed.
stops.campa: Movses Kaghankatvatsi, writing the history of the Caucasian Albanians, has Bishop Grigoris bring relics of the saint to Tsri, carrying the healer of Nicomedia over the Kur and into the Caucasus. The village is placed near Barda and the exact site is not confirmed by anything reached here. Grigoris dies about 338, which is the only handle the chronicle offers for a date. The cult is travelling east while the empire is still learning to say his name.
sources: Movses Kaghankatvatsi, History of the Caucasian Albanians, cited in en.wikipedia, 'Saint Pantaleon'
suggested_refs: Movses Kaghankatvatsi's chronicle of the Caucasian Albanians

stops.name: Amaras, the translation King Vachagan orders
stops.date_confidence: attested for a translation under Vachagan III in 489, contested as to whose relics. The Amaras Monastery record credits that king's renovation and its new chapel to the remains of St Grigoris; only the Pantaleon article reads the translation as Pantaleon's. Not resolved. Coordinates corrected from the research pool's 39.7386 / 47.1728, which is about eleven kilometres off.
stops.campa: King Vachagan the Third moves the relics from Tsri to Amaras, the monastery Gregory the Illuminator founded, one of the oldest monastic houses in the Caucasus. The Amaras record says something else: it credits the same king's renovation of 489 and its new chapel to the remains of Grigoris, and never mentions Pantaleon at all. Only the Pantaleon dossier reads the translation as his. Two articles describe one event and disagree about whose bones were in it.
suggested_refs: The 489 chapel of Vachagan III at Amaras, and the dispute over whose relics it holds

stops.name: Gorno Nerezi, the church of 1164
stops.date_confidence: attested; the church of St Panteleimon at Gorno Nerezi was built in 1164. Coordinates corrected from the research pool's 42.0083 / 21.4497, which falls on the wrong side of Skopje, about seven kilometres away. Date sharpened from the pool's '12th century'.
stops.campa: Above Skopje, on the slope at Gorno Nerezi, a church is built and dedicated to him under the Greek form of the name, Panteleimon. It is finished in 1164, and its frescoes become one of the standards by which Byzantine painting is afterward judged. There are no relics in it and none are claimed for it. It is a dedication, which by now is the commoner kind of monument to him: the East builds him churches under the name he was given at the block, and the West divides his body.
sources: en.wikipedia, 'Church of St. Panteleimon, Gorno Nerezi'
suggested_refs: The 1164 frescoes of St Panteleimon at Gorno Nerezi

stops.name: Mount Athos, the head at the Rossikon
stops.date_confidence: attested for the relic, undated for its arrival. en.wikipedia lists the head of Saint Panteleimon among the monastery's relics, which upgrades the research pool's uncorroborated note and raises the head claimants to four. The year is a placeholder. Coordinates corrected from the pool's 40.2419 / 24.2853, about seven kilometres off.
stops.campa: The Russian monastery on the west coast of Athos is dedicated to him and counts the head of Saint Panteleimon among its relics. That makes four houses claiming one skull: this one, Panachrantos on Andros, the cathedral of Lyon, and the cathedral of Vercelli. None of the four acknowledges the others. No source reached here dates the arrival of the Athonite head, and the year on this pin only stands in for the medieval Russian presence on the mountain.
suggested_refs: The Rossikon on the west coast of Athos, one of the twenty ruling monasteries

stops.name: Andros, the skull at Panachrantos
stops.date_confidence: attested as tradition; Greek Wikipedia dates the skull's arrival at Panachrantos to 1683. Coordinates corrected from the research pool's 37.8378 / 24.9297, which falls near Chora, about four and a half kilometres away; the monastery stands on Mount Gerakones at 520 metres near Fallika.
stops.campa: High on Mount Gerakones above Fallika, at five hundred and twenty metres, the monastery of Panachrantos keeps a skull it calls his and carries it out to other houses on feast days. The Greek account dates its arrival to 1683. The saint has been dead thirteen hundred and seventy-eight years and his head is on an island in the Cyclades, in a building that also does not know about Lyon, about Vercelli, or about the Rossikon on the peninsula to the north.
suggested_refs: Panachrantos Monastery on Mount Gerakones, Andros, and its feast-day processions

segments.name: West: the Division of the Body

stops.name: Lyon, the head Charlemagne is said to have brought
stops.date_confidence: the relic is attested by the Catholic Encyclopedia and en.wikipedia; the Charlemagne attribution is reconstruction only. It comes from it.wikipedia, rests on no primary document, and en.wikipedia omits it. The year is Charlemagne's imperial coronation, used as a placeholder for an attribution rather than a documented event.
stops.campa: A skull kept at the cathedral of Saint-Jean in Lyon is venerated as his. The Catholic Encyclopedia states the relic flatly; the Italian tradition adds that Charlemagne put it there, on the strength of a single sentence nobody can source, and no document supports the addition. The head at Vercelli, four hundred kilometres away, is the same head.
suggested_refs: The head relic at the Cathedral of Saint-Jean, Lyon

stops.name: Cologne, the abbey church consecrated to him
stops.date_confidence: attested; Archbishop Bruno added the Benedictine abbey in 955 and the church was consecrated in 980. Pin inherited byte-identical from catorce_santos_ayudantes.journey.json. Corrections carried: the research pool gave a ninth-century foundation and two wrong coordinates, and asserted relics here. en.wikipedia names only shrines of Alban and Maurinus and documents no Pantaleon relic.
stops.campa: On the Rhine, over a Roman villa, Archbishop Bruno's Benedictine abbey church is consecrated to Pantaleon in 980. Theophanu, the Byzantine wife of Otto the Second and mother of Otto the Third, orders its westwork built and asks to be buried in it, and is. English scholarship calls this the oldest church of his cult west of Byzantium. It names shrines of Alban and Maurinus inside and no relic of Pantaleon, so the oldest western house of his cult may hold nothing of him.
suggested_refs: St Pantaleon, Cologne, its Ottonian westwork and the tomb of Theophanu

stops.name: Saint-Denis, among the royal hoard
stops.date_confidence: the relics are attested by the Catholic Encyclopedia and en.wikipedia, with no date, no account of arrival, and no body part named. The year is an admitted placeholder set in Suger's century, when the abbey's hoard is being catalogued rather than acquired. Pin inherited byte-identical from catorce_santos_ayudantes.journey.json.
stops.campa: Bodily relics of Pantaleon are venerated at the abbey of Saint-Denis outside Paris, gathered into the largest relic collection in France, in the same church that keeps Denis's own severed head. The Catholic Encyclopedia records the relics and gives no date, no account of how they came, and no description of which part of him is there. The year on this pin is a placeholder set in Suger's century, when the abbey's hoard is being catalogued rather than acquired.
suggested_refs: The relic treasury of the abbey of Saint-Denis

stops.name: Vercelli, the second head
stops.date_confidence: attested by it.wikipedia as a claim, undated by it; the year is a placeholder. The claim stands in direct contradiction with Lyon, Andros and the Rossikon, and no source reached in this research attempts a ruling between the four.
stops.campa: The cathedral of Vercelli in Piedmont claims his head. Lyon claims his head. The Italian and the French traditions are each perfectly clear and neither has heard of the other, and Andros and the Rossikon make it four. The Piedmontese claim is undated in the source that carries it. No source reached in this research attempts a ruling between the four of them. Four churches in four countries keep a skull under his name, and at most one of them can be holding it.
suggested_refs: The head relic claimed by the Duomo di Vercelli

stops.name: Venice, the arm at San Pantalon
stops.date_confidence: the arm relic is attested by it.wikipedia and undated by it; the year is a placeholder. Coordinates corrected from the research pool's 45.4351 / 12.3232. The claim that the church's name produced the commedia dell'arte mask Pantalone is not in the cited article and is dropped as contested folk etymology.
stops.campa: In Dorsoduro a church carries his name in the Venetian form, San Pantalon, and keeps an arm bone. Its ceiling will later be covered by Fumiani with an apotheosis of the saint painted across the whole vault, one of the largest painted surfaces in the city. The claim that the church's name produced the mask Pantalone of the commedia dell'arte is not in the sources cited for it. It is a contested folk etymology, and it is dropped here rather than repeated.
suggested_refs: Fumiani's ceiling apotheosis at San Pantalon, Dorsoduro

stops.name: Regensburg, the fourteen assemble after the plague
stops.date_confidence: attested for the mid-fourteenth-century formation of the group in the German dioceses; the exact year is the atlas's working convention. English scholarship names the Rhineland for the devotion's origin and German scholarship names Regensburg, and the atlas carries both. Pin inherited byte-identical from saint_acacius.journey.json and saint_barbara.journey.json.
stops.campa: After the Black Death the German dioceses fix him into a company of fourteen helpers, each with an office. He takes physicians and midwives, and the protection of domestic animals, and is invoked against cancer and consumption. Barbara, Blaise, Catherine, Christopher, Cyriacus, Denis, Erasmus, Eustace, George, Giles, Margaret, Vitus and Acacius stand with him. German scholarship names Regensburg for the origin and English scholarship names the Rhineland, and both are kept here rather than adjudicated.
stops.quote: Domestic animals, too, being attacked by the plague, Sts. George, Erasmus, Pantaleon, and Vitus were invoked for their protection.
stops.quote_source: Bonaventure Hammer, Mary, Help of Christians, and the Fourteen Saints Invoked as Holy Helpers (1908), Part III
suggested_refs: The mid-fourteenth-century formation of the Fourteen Holy Helpers in the German dioceses

stops.name: Nuremberg, the order closes at fourteen
stops.date_confidence: attested as about 1400 by de.wikipedia; the exact date is the atlas's working convention, shared verbatim with catorce_santos_ayudantes.journey.json, saint_acacius.journey.json and saint_cyriacus.journey.json, and the pin is inherited byte-identical from them. The three surviving Western feast dates are attested and unharmonized.
stops.campa: By about the turn of the century the list is closed, and the same fourteen appear in the same order across Regensburg, Bamberg, Wurzburg and Nuremberg. Pantaleon stands in it between Margaret and Vitus. The physician of Nicomedia, dead eleven hundred years, is now an item with a fixed position in a German devotional sequence. His feast is the twenty-seventh of July in both calendars, with a twenty-eighth of July and an eighteenth of February surviving in some Western books.
suggested_refs: The closed late-medieval sequence of the fourteen, and the unharmonized feast dates

stops.name: Ravello, the ampoule on the Amalfi coast
stops.date_confidence: tradition; it.wikipedia traces the custody of the Ravello ampoule to the twelfth century and the year here is a placeholder at the start of it. The liquefaction claim contradicts the Catholic Encyclopedia's placing of the same miracle at Constantinople; neither source acknowledges the other. Liguori's testimony reaches this file through en.wikipedia's quotation, not the original edition.
stops.campa: In the cathedral of Ravello, on the cliff above Amalfi, a vial of dried blood is kept, its custody traced by local tradition to the twelfth century. Every twenty-seventh of July it is reported to liquefy, and the coast road fills with people who have come for it. Alphonsus Liguori writes that he saw the blood in that state himself. Richard Wagner will climb to this town in 1880 and find Klingsor's magic garden in the Villa Rufolo, a few streets from the relic, and never mention it.
stops.quote: At Ravello, a city in the kingdom of Naples, there is a vial of his blood, which becomes blood every year [on his feastday], and may be seen in this state interspersed with the milk, as I, the author of this work, have seen it.
stops.quote_source: St. Alphonsus Liguori, Victories of the Martyrs, life of St. Pantaleon, quoted in the English Wikipedia article 'Saint Pantaleon'
suggested_refs: The blood ampoule of the Duomo di Ravello and its annual liquefaction

stops.name: Porto, the Armenians at Miragaia
stops.date_confidence: attested by en.wikipedia: Armenian refugees fleeing the fall of Constantinople carry relics to the church of Sao Pedro de Miragaia at Porto. The month and day are placeholders on the year of the fall.
stops.campa: Armenian refugees leaving Constantinople after the fall carry relics of Pantaleon west and put them in the church of Sao Pedro de Miragaia, on the Douro waterfront at Porto. The relics have gone from Nicomedia into the capital, and out of the capital in the same season the capital ends. This is the most precisely dated leg of the whole dispersal, and it exists because an empire collapsed and the people running from it took with them what was portable.
suggested_refs: The church of Sao Pedro de Miragaia, Porto, first western home of the Porto relics

stops.name: Putna, the Moldavian relics
stops.date_confidence: attested by OrthodoxWiki and it.wikipedia for relics at Putna in Bucovina and at the Ss. Peter and Paul Cathedral in Constanta; neither transfer is dated in any source reached, and the year is a placeholder taken from Putna's own foundation under Stephen the Great.
stops.campa: Relics of him rest at Putna in Bucovina, the monastery Stephen the Great founded, and at the cathedral of Saints Peter and Paul at Constanta on the Black Sea. Neither transfer is dated in the sources reached here, and the pin takes Putna's foundation years as a placeholder. Orthodox Romania keeps him as a healer, which is the office the East has given him without a break since Nicomedia. The West gave him instead a fixed rank in a numbered list of fourteen.
suggested_refs: Putna Monastery in Bucovina, and the Ss. Peter and Paul Cathedral at Constanta

stops.name: Porto, the cathedral takes them
stops.date_confidence: attested; en.wikipedia dates the transfer from Miragaia to Porto Cathedral to 1499. Month and day are placeholders.
stops.campa: In 1499 the relics are carried up the hill from Miragaia into the Se, and Porto takes him as a civic patron. Forty-six years after the Armenians landed he is diocesan property rather than refugee property, and his feast becomes a municipal date. The cathedral that receives him is granite, and was fortified before anyone thought to decorate it. A physician born on the Sea of Marmara is the patron of an Atlantic port, twelve hundred years after his death.
suggested_refs: The Se do Porto and the civic patronage of Sao Pantaleao

stops.name: Madrid, the vial at the Encarnacion
stops.date_confidence: the vial is attested by es.wikipedia; its acquisition is undated in every source reached, and the year here is the foundation of the convent, used as a placeholder. Provenance contradiction flagged: it.wikipedia counts Madrid among the Ravello gifts, while es.wikipedia's article on the Ermita de San Pantaleon de Losa in Burgos says the Madrid ampoule came from there. Coordinates corrected from the pool's 40.4183 / -3.7144.
stops.campa: In the royal convent Queen Margaret of Austria founded beside the Alcazar, a vial of his blood is kept, and it is said to liquefy every twenty-sixth of July, one day before Ravello's. The Spanish account of its origin does not point to Ravello at all: it says the Madrid ampoule came from the hermitage of San Pantaleon de Losa in Burgos. Two provenances for one vial, in the same national encyclopedia, on different pages, and neither page mentions the other.
sources: es.wikipedia, 'Ermita de San Pantaleon de Losa'
suggested_refs: The Real Monasterio de la Encarnacion, Madrid, and its 26 July liquefaction

stops.name: Ravello, Bishop Panicola's chapel and the crack
stops.date_confidence: attested by it.wikipedia for the 1643 transfer in solemn procession by Bishop Bernardino Panicola; month and day are placeholders. The cracking of the glass is dated by the same source only to the seventeenth century and is folded into this stop.
stops.campa: Bernardino Panicola, bishop of Ravello, has a new chapel built for the blood and moves it there in solemn procession. Within the same century the glass of the vial cracks, and the crack is still visible in it today. The relic that is famous for changing state is now housed in a container that is itself damaged, and neither the damage nor the liquefaction is treated by the tradition as a reason to open the thing and look inside. The crack is catalogued and left where it is.
suggested_refs: The 1643 chapel of the blood at Ravello, and the cracked seventeenth-century vial

stops.name: Ravello, the eight ampoules sent out
stops.date_confidence: attested for the recipients by it.wikipedia, undated for any of the gifts; the year is a placeholder. Correction carried: the research pool listed four recipients. The source names eight, and Martignano, Caiazzo, Lanciano and Irsina were omitted.
stops.campa: Later bishops of Ravello divide the relic and send portions out: to Constantinople, Montauro, Martignano, Limbadi, Caiazzo, Lanciano, Irsina, and the Monasterio de la Encarnacion in Madrid. Eight secondary ampoules, each said to answer the Ravello one and liquefy in sympathy with it. The Italian source lists all eight recipients by name and dates none of the gifts. Constantinople is on the list, which sends the blood back to the city already keeping a phial of it.

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the sanctuary at Mataderos
stops.date_confidence: attested by es.wikipedia, which names the Mataderos sanctuary, the arm fragment, and Cardinal Albino Luciani as donor through the Venetian see; the year is a placeholder inside Luciani's patriarchate of Venice, which the source does not narrow. Correction carried: the research pool called the church unnamed and pinned the city centre, but the cited source names it.
stops.campa: In the Mataderos neighbourhood a sanctuary holds a bone fragment said to come from his arm, given by Cardinal Albino Luciani through the see of Venice, before he was Pope John Paul the First for thirty-three days. Venice had the arm; Buenos Aires has a piece of it. The date on this pin is a placeholder inside Luciani's Venetian patriarchate, which the source does not narrow. Queues form here on the twenty-seventh of July long enough to close the street.
suggested_refs: The Santuario de San Pantaleon in Mataderos, Buenos Aires, and its 27 July queues

stops.name: Ravello, the seventeenth of March 2020
stops.date_confidence: attested as a report by it.wikipedia: an extraordinary liquefaction during a livestreamed prayer service amid the COVID-19 pandemic. No independent scientific report on the event was located. Gregorian date, on a journey whose earlier stops are Julian.
stops.campa: Italy is shut. The cathedral is empty and the prayers are livestreamed, and during the service the blood in the cracked vial is reported to liquefy, four months out of season. No independent report on the event was located. The other ampoules keep their July date; this one runs in March, with the doors locked. The physician of Nicomedia is being asked for help against a plague through a camera, seventeen hundred and fifteen years after his colleagues turned him in.
suggested_refs: The livestreamed liquefaction of 17 March 2020 at Ravello
